# Mem3R: Streaming 3D Reconstruction with Hybrid Memory

**Authors:** Changkun Liu Affiliation: Google Affiliation: The Hong Kong University of Science and Technology Jiezhi Yang Affiliation: Google Zeman Li Affiliation: Google Yuan Deng Affiliation: Google Jiancong Guo Affiliation: Google Binbin Xu Affiliation: Google Luca Ballan Affiliation: Google

## Abstract

Streaming 3D perception is well suited to robotics and augmented reality, where long visual streams must be processed efficiently and consistently. Recent recurrent models offer a promising solution by maintaining fixed-size states and enabling linear-time inference, but they often suffer from temporal forgetting over long sequences due to the limited capacity of compressed memories. We propose Mem3R, a streaming 3D reconstruction model with a hybrid memory design that decouples camera tracking from geometric mapping to improve temporal consistency over long sequences. For camera tracking, Mem3R employs an implicit fast-weight memory implemented as a lightweight Multi-Layer Perceptron updated via Test-Time Training. For geometric mapping, Mem3R maintains an explicit token-based fixed-size state. Compared with CUT3R, this design not only significantly improves long-sequence performance but also reduces the model size from 793M to 644M parameters. Mem3R supports existing improved plug-and-play state update strategies developed for CUT3R. Specifically, Mem3R combined with TTT3R reduces absolute trajectory error by up to 39% relative to CUT3R combined with TTT3R on 500- to 1000-frame sequences from the TUM Dynamics dataset. The resulting improvements also extend to other downstream tasks, including video depth estimation and 3D reconstruction. Project page: https://lck666666.github.io/Mem3R/.

*Figure 1: Mem3R is an RNN-based model built on the CUT3R paradigm that achieves stronger long-sequence streaming 3D perception. Built on a dual-memory design, Mem3R combines (i) an implicit memory $\mathcal{W}$ for camera pose estimation and (ii) an explicit memory of persistent tokens for global geometric context. Mem3R is further compatible with plug-and-play state-update strategies developed for CUT3R, such as TTT3R.*

## 1 Introduction

A central challenge in real-time 3D perception is to recover accurate scene geometry and camera motion from long visual streams under strict computational and memory budgets. This capability is essential for a wide range of mobile applications, including robotic visual localization, navigation, and augmented reality. Recent progress in feed-forward multi-view geometry, driven by models such as DUSt3R [63] and VGGT [61], has inspired a new wave of Transformer-based architectures [33, 55, 71, 80, 65, 49] that achieve impressive performance in 3D reconstruction and pose estimation. However, these methods typically rely on global pairwise alignment or dense cross-frame attention, leading to computational costs that scale quadratically with sequence length and limit their applicability in long-horizon streaming scenarios.

To enable scalable streaming, prior work has mainly evolved along two directions. The first line of work leverages causal-attention Key-Value (KV) caches to preserve the full observation history [60, 32, 77, 85]. While effective, this paradigm incurs memory consumption that grows linearly with sequence length, making it increasingly vulnerable to out-of-memory (OOM) failures during long-horizon inference. The second direction, exemplified by CUT3R, adopts a Recurrent Neural Network (RNN)-based architecture with a fixed-size latent state, enabling constant-memory inference. However, this compact state also creates an information bottleneck: once the sequence length exceeds the typical training horizon, CUT3R suffers from substantial temporal forgetting and trajectory drift. To alleviate these issues, TTT3R [14] reinterprets state updates through the perspective of Test-Time Training (TTT) and introduces per-token update weights that emphasize tokens most relevant to the current observations. Building on this idea, subsequent works [83, 18] have proposed alternative plug-and-play update strategies to further improve CUT3R.

In this work, we present Mem3R, an enhanced RNN-based architecture with a dual-memory design for long-horizon streaming 3D perception. Our key idea is to improve the representational efficiency of the recurrent state by decoupling camera tracking from geometric mapping. Specifically, Mem3R replaces CUT3R’s pose-related token memory and its Transformer-based memory read/write blocks (implemented as the LocalMemory module in the official CUT3R codebase) with a lightweight implicit Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP)-based memory for pose estimation via TTT inspired by LaCT [81], while retaining an explicit token-based memory to preserve global geometric context. This dual-memory design yields a more compact and effective backbone, reducing the parameter count from 793M to 644M (a 19% reduction) while achieving stronger performance, as illustrated in Fig. 1. We also introduce a learnable channel-wise state update module, inspired by recent advances in finite-state RNN architectures [56, 5], to enable finer-grained control over state updates.

As a result, Mem3R remains fully compatible with training-free per-token state-update strategies such as TTT3R [14] and TTSA3R [83], and it delivers further gains when combined with them. Across camera pose estimation, video depth estimation, and 3D reconstruction, Mem3R shows clear improvements in most evaluated settings while preserving the inference speed and constant-memory advantages of RNN-based streaming models. These results establish Mem3R as a stronger and more memory-efficient backbone for long-sequence streaming 3D perception.

#### Offline Feed-forward 3D Reconstruction.

DUSt3R [63] proposes an end-to-end, feed-forward approach to 3D reconstruction, directly regressing point maps from image pairs. Subsequent extensions [33, 28, 38, 20, 13, 78, 70, 15, 21] broadened this formulation to more challenging settings, but most remain fundamentally pairwise and therefore require costly global alignment once more than two views are involved. To overcome this limitation, recent offline multiview models [80, 71, 61, 65, 49, 22, 31] employ large feed-forward Transformers with global attention to jointly process all input views and predict per-view geometry and camera poses in a single forward pass. Representative examples such as VGGT [61] achieve strong reconstruction quality, but their computational and memory costs scale quadratically with the number of frames. Moreover, they are inefficient for streaming data, as incorporating a newly arrived view typically requires reprocessing the entire sequence. Although methods such as FastVGGT [49] reduce inference overhead through token merging, these approaches remain better suited to offline reconstruction than to real-time long-sequence streaming settings.

#### Online 3D Reconstruction.

Online 3D reconstruction methods [60, 77, 32, 85, 62, 67, 36, 16] process views incrementally and update scene representations on the fly, making them attractive for robotics and embodied perception. Existing approaches mainly differ in how they preserve historical context. Causal-cache methods, such as StreamVGGT [85], retain past keys and values for long-range temporal conditioning, but their memory and computation still grow with sequence length. In contrast, recurrent methods such as CUT3R [62] maintain a fixed-size latent state for constant-memory inference. However, compressing long-term observations into a compact state creates an information bottleneck, often causing temporal forgetting and drift on long sequences. Recent training-free update strategies, including TTT3R [14] and TTSA3R [83], improve CUT3R-style recurrent updates, while Point3R [67] enhances memory recall through explicit 3D point associations at the cost of memory growth. In contrast, our method improves the representational efficiency of the recurrent backbone through a dual-memory design, while remaining compatible with plug-and-play update strategies such as TTT3R and TTSA3R.

#### Fast Weight Programs and Memory Architectures.

The view of linear layers as associative memories dates back to Hopfield networks [25] and was later developed in fast weight programmers, where dynamic fast programs are integrated into recurrent neural networks as writable memory stores [45, 46, 47]. Building upon these foundational concepts, modern sequence modeling has diverged into two primary structural paradigms: linear memory modules and deep memory modules. Linear memory modules [24, 42, 73, 72, 26, 56] maintain matrix-valued hidden states with linear state transitions, while deep memory modules [5, 7, 35, 54, 8, 6, 81] use online-adapted sub-networks with dynamically updated parameters to encode contextual information. Our method is particularly inspired by this latter line of work, using an online-adapted implicit memory to improve long-horizon performance. Concurrent works [59, 79, 29] also incorporate TTT memory layers into 3D perception but address different settings: tttLRM [59] targets novel view synthesis with 3D Gaussian Splatting, [29, 19, 69] focus on faster offline reconstruction, and LoGeR [79] studies chunk-wise reconstruction with sliding-window attention rather than frame-by-frame streaming reconstruction.

## 3 Method

In streaming 3D perception, a model processes an image sequence $\{I_{t}\}_{t=1}^{N}$ incrementally, estimating camera motion and scene geometry online as new observations arrive.

### 3.1 Overview

We begin by briefly reviewing the recurrent state formulation in CUT3R to highlight the key differences in our design:

$$ X^{\prime}_{t},\bar{S}_{t}=\mathrm{Decoders}(X_{t},S_{t-1}), $$

where $S_{t-1}$ is the state at time $t-1$ , $\bar{S}_{t}$ is the updated state produced directly by the decoder, and $X_{t}=[z_{t},F_{t}]$ consists of a learnable pose token $z_{t}$ and image tokens $F_{t}$ extracted from the current frame $I_{t}$ .

Our Mem3R is also an RNN-based architecture that maintains a fixed-size recurrent state for online 3D perception. The key idea is to improve the efficiency of the recurrent memory representation by replacing the pose-related components of the recurrent state and transformer-based decoder blocks with an implicit MLP. To this end, Mem3R uses a hybrid memory design: an implicit memory $\mathcal{W}$ , implemented as an MLP-based fast-weight module for camera tracking, and an explicit memory $S$ , implemented as persistent state tokens for geometric mapping, as shown in Fig. 1 and Fig. 2. Unlike CUT3R, which directly writes decoder outputs into the recurrent state, our model treats the state output from the decoder as a candidate update and integrates it with a learnable channel-wise gate.

At time $t$ , the current frame is encoded into visual tokens $F_{t}$ . The implicit memory predicts a pose token prior $\hat{p}_{t}$ , which is processed together with $F_{t}$ and the previous explicit state $S_{t-1}$ by a transformer decoder. The decoder produces a posterior pose token $p_{t}$ , updated visual features $F^{\prime}_{t}$ , and a candidate state update $S^{\prime}_{t}$ . The implicit memory is then updated online by aligning prior $\hat{p}_{t}$ with posterior $p_{t}$ , while the explicit memory is updated through channel-wise gated integration of $S^{\prime}_{t}$ .

### 3.2 Implicit Memory via Test-Time Training

To improve long-horizon camera tracking while preserving a constant inference speed, we introduce an adaptive fast-weight memory implemented as a lightweight SwiGLU MLP [48]:

$$ f_{\mathcal{W}}(x)=W_{2}\Big(\mathrm{SiLU}(W_{1}x)\odot(W_{3}x)\Big), $$

where $\mathcal{W}=\{W_{1},W_{2},W_{3}\}$ denotes the fast weights updated online during inference.

Given the current visual tokens $F_{t}$ , we first compute a $L_{2}$ -normalized query feature $\kappa_{t}$ and read a pose prior from the previous fast weights $\mathcal{W}_{t-1}$ :

$$ \hat{p}_{t}=f_{\mathcal{W}_{t-1}}(\kappa_{t}). $$

This prior replaces CUT3R’s learned pose token $z_{t}$ , yielding $X_{t}=[\hat{p}_{t},F_{t}].$ The decoder then produces

$$ X^{\prime}_{t},S^{\prime}_{t}=\mathrm{Decoders}(X_{t},S_{t-1}), $$

where $X^{\prime}_{t}=[p_{t},F^{\prime}_{t}]$ , with $p_{t}$ defined as the refined posterior pose token and $F^{\prime}_{t}$ as the state-enriched visual features.

We update the implicit memory by aligning the prior and posterior:

$$ \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{ttt}}(\hat{p}_{t},p_{t})=\langle\hat{p}_{t},p_{t}\rangle. $$

To make the update adaptive for different $I_{t}$ , we predict a per-step decay factor $\alpha_{t}=1-\gamma\cdot\sigma(W_{\alpha}F_{t})$ and per-layer learning rates $\eta_{t}$ from the current features:

$$ \eta_{t}=\mathrm{Softplus}\!\left(W_{\eta}F_{t}+\mathrm{Softplus}^{-1}(\eta_{\mathrm{base}})\right), $$

where $\gamma=0.01$ is the decay scale and $\eta_{\mathrm{base}}=0.001$ is the base learning rate. Here, $\mathrm{Softplus}^{-1}(x)=\log(e^{x}-1)$ ensures that $\eta_{t}=\eta_{\mathrm{base}}$ when $W_{\eta}F_{t}=0$ . $\sigma(\cdot)$ denotes the sigmoid function. The fast weights are then updated by

$$ \mathcal{W}_{t}=\alpha_{t}\mathcal{W}_{t-1}+\eta_{t}\odot\nabla_{\mathcal{W}}\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{ttt}}. $$

This update enables the model to estimate accurate pose cues while filtering out transient noise, effectively turning the fast-weight module into a compact implicit temporal memory for robust camera tracking. We provide more details about this module in the supplementary material.

Moreover, when combined with the training-free, plug-and-play state update strategies TTT3R or TTSA3R, Mem3R further yields better results compared to applying these strategies to CUT3R.*

### 3.3 Channel-wise Update of Explicit Memory

To represent persistent global geometry, we retain an explicit token-based memory $S_{t}\in\mathbb{R}^{N_{s}\times C},$ where $N_{s}$ is the number of state tokens and $C$ is the channel dimension. The decoder output $S^{\prime}_{t}$ in Eq. 4 is treated as a candidate state update rather than the final new state.

Directly overwriting the state can lead to temporal forgetting in long sequences. To address this issue, we introduce a channel-wise update gate $\zeta_{t}\in(0,1)^{N_{s}\times C}$ :

$$ \zeta_{t}=\sigma\!\left(f_{\zeta}(F_{t},S_{t-1})\right), $$

where $f_{\zeta}$ is an MLP. The explicit memory is then updated as

$$ S_{t}=\zeta_{t}\odot S^{\prime}_{t}+(1-\zeta_{t})\odot S_{t-1}. $$

This channel-wise gating enables finer control over memory evolution, allowing stable geometric features to be preserved while selectively integrating new observations. During inference, when applying the per-token state-update mechanism of TTT3R or TTSA3R, we combine its per-token gate $G_{t}$ with our channel-wise gate $\zeta_{t}$ to obtain the final update gate. The state is updated as

$$ S_{t}=G_{t}\odot\zeta_{t}\odot S^{\prime}_{t}+\left(1-G_{t}\odot\zeta_{t}\right)\odot S_{t-1}, $$

where $G_{t}\in\mathbb{R}^{N_{s}\times 1}$ is broadcast along the channel dimension and controls token-level updates, while $\zeta_{t}\in(0,1)^{N_{s}\times C}$ controls channel-level updates. We provide more details on this module in the supplementary material.

### 3.4 Prediction Heads and Training

We follow CUT3R in using the same prediction heads and supervision. Given the refined tokens $(p_{t},F^{\prime}_{t})$ , Mem3R predicts local-frame pointmaps and confidence scores, $(\hat{Z}_{t}^{\mathrm{self}},C_{t}^{\mathrm{self}})=\mathrm{Head}_{\mathrm{self}}(F^{\prime}_{t})$ , world-frame pointmaps and confidence scores, $(\hat{Z}_{t}^{\mathrm{world}},C_{t}^{\mathrm{world}})=\mathrm{Head}_{\mathrm{world}}(p_{t},F^{\prime}_{t}),$ and the 6-DoF camera pose $\hat{P}_{t}=\mathrm{Head}_{\mathrm{pose}}(p_{t}).$

For training, we use the same objectives as CUT3R. The local- and world-frame pointmaps are supervised with the confidence-aware 3D regression loss in CUT3R and MASt3R [33]:

$$ \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{3D}}=\sum_{f\in\{\mathrm{self},\mathrm{world}\}}\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{conf}}\!\left(\hat{Z}^{f},Z^{f},C^{f}\right). $$

$$ \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{conf}}(\hat{Z},Z,C)=\sum_{(\hat{z},z,c)\in(\hat{Z},Z,C)}\left(c\cdot\left\lVert\frac{\hat{z}}{\hat{s}}-\frac{z}{s}\right\rVert_{2}-\beta\log c\right), $$

where $\hat{s}$ and $s$ are scale normalization factors for $\hat{Z}$ and ${Z}$ , respectively.

Camera pose is supervised by $\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{pose}}=\sum_{t=1}^{N}\left(\left\lVert\hat{q}_{t}-q_{t}\right\rVert_{2}+\left\lVert\frac{\hat{\tau}_{t}}{\hat{s}}-\frac{\tau_{t}}{s}\right\rVert_{2}\right),$ and, when raymap inputs are available, we additionally use the RGB reconstruction loss $\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{rgb}}=\left\lVert\hat{I}_{r}-I_{r}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}.$ The full objective is $\mathcal{L}=\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{3D}}+\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{pose}}+\mathbbm{1}_{\mathrm{raymap}}\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{rgb}},$ where $\mathbbm{1}_{\mathrm{raymap}}$ indicates whether the input is a raymap.

To ensure that the gains can be fairly attributed to our architectural design, we train Mem3R using the same 26-dataset mixture and training configuration as the final training stage of CUT3R, with input sequences ranging from 4 to 64 views. The training data cover diverse real and synthetic scenes, including CO3Dv2 [43], ARKitScenes [3], MegaDepth [34], MapFree [1], DL3DV [37], and Hypersim [44]. The full dataset list is provided in the supplementary material. We initialize the encoder, decoders, and prediction heads from pre-trained 512-DPT CUT3R weights and fine-tune all modules except the encoder. Optimization is performed with AdamW [39], using an initial learning rate of $1\times 10^{-6}$ , linear warmup, and cosine decay. Training takes approximately 10 hours on 32 NVIDIA H100 GPUs with a batch size of 8 per GPU.

## 4 Experiment

*Figure 4: Qualitative visualization of predicted camera trajectories on the TUM Dynamics dataset (top row) and the ScanNet dataset (bottom row). Each row is evaluated on the same sequence. Our Mem3R achieves significant improvement compared with CUT3R. Moreover, when combined with TTT3R or TTSA3R, Mem3R further reduces drift compared to applying these strategies to CUT3R.*

We evaluate our Mem3R on a variety of tasks, including camera pose estimation (Sec. 4.1), video depth estimation (Sec. 4.2), and 3D reconstruction (Sec. 4.3). We primarily focus on streaming 3D reconstruction models, specifically Point3R [67], StreamVGGT [85], and CUT3R [62]. Among these, we treat the RNN-based CUT3R as our closest baseline to demonstrate that Mem3R achieves superior performance on long sequences ( $\geq$ 200 frames). Furthermore, we show that Mem3R is fully compatible with existing training-free state update mechanisms developed for CUT3R, such as TTT3R [14] and TTSA3R [83]. Quantitative accuracy results are obtained using NVIDIA A100 40GB GPUs. Qualitative visualizations and efficiency measurements are conducted separately on a workstation equipped with a single NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell Max-Q GPU.

### 4.1 Camera Pose Estimation

Following [14, 83], we evaluate camera pose accuracy on the TUM Dynamics [52] and ScanNet [17] datasets using sequences ranging from 50 to 1,000 frames. We adopt the standard Absolute Trajectory Error (ATE) metric, computed after Sim(3) alignment [58] between the estimated and ground-truth trajectories. As illustrated in Fig. 3, Mem3R consistently outperforms CUT3R and Point3R. Furthermore, integrating TTT3R and TTSA3R into Mem3R yields significantly lower pose errors, particularly on sequences exceeding 400 streaming frames. In contrast, VGGT and StreamVGGT, both based on full attention, are prone to memory exhaustion for such long sequences. Qualitative comparisons in Fig. 4 demonstrate that Mem3R, when equipped with TTT3R and TTSA3R, achieves superior tracking accuracy compared to CUT3R under identical state-update strategies.

Notably, from Fig. 3, Mem3R with TTT3R provides a 39% relative reduction in ATE at the 500-frame mark on the TUM dynamics dataset compared with the base TTT3R model. More results including short sequences are provided in the supplementary material.

### 4.2 Video Depth Estimation

As in [78, 62], we evaluate long-sequence video depth estimation on the KITTI [23] and Bonn [41] datasets. These datasets span 300 to 500 frames and encompass a diverse range of dynamic, static, indoor, and outdoor scenes. We report both scale-invariant and metric-scale results using the Absolute Relative error (Abs Rel) and the $\delta_{1.25}$ threshold (the percentage of pixels where $\max(\frac{d_{gt}}{d_{est}},\frac{d_{est}}{d_{gt}})<1.25$ ). As demonstrated in Tabs. 1 and 2, Mem3R significantly outperforms CUT3R. Integrating Mem3R with TTT3R and TTSA3R further yields performance gains across most scenarios. Furthermore, we evaluate short-sequence performance (50 streaming frames) on the Sintel [10] dataset in the supplementary material.

### 4.3 3D Reconstruction

We evaluate our multiview reconstruction framework on the 7-Scenes [50] dataset over sequences of 50 to 400 frames, using Chamfer Distance (CD) and Normal Consistency (NC) as the primary metrics. Following TTT3R [14], CD is defined as the mean of accuracy and completeness, where accuracy measures the Euclidean distance from reconstructed points to the nearest ground-truth points and completeness is defined conversely. As shown in Fig. 5, Mem3R significantly outperforms CUT3R. Moreover, when combined with TTT3R or TTSA3R, Mem3R consistently achieves lower CD than Point3R and CUT3R under the same state-update strategy, further validating the effectiveness of our architecture. Qualitative results in Figs. 6 and 1 show that Mem3R produces more accurate and better-aligned 3D reconstructions, with further improvements when combined with TTT3R or TTSA3R. For example, in Fig. 1, Ours + TTT3R reconstructs the staircase with more accurate step spacing and clearer handrails. Additional visualizations and results on NRGBD [2] are reported in the supplementary material.

### 4.4 Model Efficiency

Mem3R maintains constant GPU memory complexity with respect to sequence length. As shown in Tab. 3, Mem3R matches the throughput of CUT3R and its training-free state update variants while reducing GPU memory usage by 7% and parameter count by 19% relative to CUT3R. All evaluations are conducted on a workstation with a single NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell Max-Q GPU using $512\times 384$ images from 7-Scenes.

## 5 Conclusion

Mem3R is an RNN-based hybrid memory model for streaming 3D reconstruction that decouples camera tracking from geometric mapping, improving long-term consistency and long-sequence performance while preserving recurrent streaming efficiency. Compared with CUT3R, Mem3R is also more parameter-efficient, reducing the model size from 793M to 644M parameters. Despite being more compact, it significantly lowers the Absolute Trajectory Error (ATE) on the challenging 500-1000 frame benchmark of the TUM Dynamics and ScanNet datasets. The resulting improvements also extend to downstream tasks such as 3D reconstruction and video depth estimation. These results establish hybrid memory as an effective design for accurate and efficient long-horizon 3D perception.

### 6.1 Design Insight and Architectural Novelty

Mem3R is not a direct combination of CUT3R [62] and test-time training. Existing training-free adaptation approaches typically retain the original CUT3R architecture and modify only the inference-time state-update rule. In contrast, Mem3R redesigns and retrains the recurrent memory architecture itself. The key design question is not simply whether test-time adaptation can be introduced, but rather which part of the recurrent state should be represented by an adaptive implicit memory, which information should remain explicitly stored, and how these different memory components should be updated.

Our design is motivated by the different characteristics of camera pose and dense scene geometry. Camera pose is a compact $6$ -DoF state with strong temporal continuity, whereas dense geometry is high-dimensional and must preserve surface structure, depth, local geometric details, and cross-view correspondences accumulated over time. CUT3R maintains an explicit geometric state and a separate Transformer-based LocalMemory for pose-related information. We replace the latter with a lightweight fast-weight memory while retaining the explicit geometric state.

Based on this observation, Mem3R decomposes the recurrent memory according to the information being represented. We selectively replace only the pose-related LocalMemory in CUT3R with a lightweight fast-weight memory, in which pose-related temporal information is represented implicitly through rapidly adapted model parameters. In contrast, we retain an explicit token-based state for dense geometry, since geometric information must preserve rich spatial structure accumulated across frames. We further introduce a channel-wise state update gate to regulate how newly observed geometric features are incorporated into the persistent geometric state.

This leads to three central architectural design choices:

- 1. Which recurrent state should use test-time adaptive memory. We apply fast-weight adaptation specifically to the pose-related state rather than replacing the entire recurrent memory.

- 2. How different information should be represented. Pose is represented by a compact implicit adaptive memory, while dense geometry remains explicitly represented by state tokens.

- 3. How persistent geometric memory should be updated. Instead of uniformly overwriting or updating the geometric state, the proposed channel-wise gate adaptively controls information retention and incorporation at the feature-channel level.

The ablation results in the main paper support these design choices. Removing either the fast-weight pose memory or the channel-wise state update gate consistently degrades performance, while combining both components yields the strongest long-horizon results. Moreover, as analyzed in Sec. 6.2, Mem3R reduces the total parameter count from approximately $793$ M to $644$ M. Therefore, the observed improvement does not arise from increasing model capacity; instead, it results from using a more suitable memory representation and update mechanism for the different types of recurrent state.

Overall, the contribution of Mem3R is not the generic application of test-time training to an existing recurrent reconstruction model, but a structured redesign of its memory architecture. By separating low-dimensional pose dynamics from high-dimensional geometric state, and assigning each an appropriate representation and update mechanism, Mem3R achieves both improved long-horizon performance and substantially reduced model complexity.

### 6.2 Model Details

The explicit geometric memory consists of $768$ state tokens, each with a feature dimension of $768$ . We set the confidence regularization coefficient $\beta$ in Eq. 12 to $0.2$ . In this section, we provide additional architectural details of the lightweight fast-weight implicit memory introduced in Sec. 3.2 and the channel-wise state update module described in Sec. 3.3. We further analyze the source of the parameter reduction compared with the original pose-related LocalMemory module in CUT3R [62].

#### Fast-weight memory via TTT.

The fast-weight module serves as the core implicit memory for pose tracking and contains approximately $1.56$ M parameters. It first projects the $1024$ -dimensional visual features into a $768$ -dimensional latent space, which is evenly divided into $12$ heads with a head dimension of $64$ . The memory is implemented using a SwiGLU-based parameterization $\mathcal{W}=\{W_{1},W_{2},W_{3}\}$ , where $W_{1},W_{2},W_{3}\in\mathbb{R}^{64\times 64}$ for each head.

Its online update is controlled by two lightweight linear predictors. The learning-rate head outputs $36$ scalars, corresponding to three learning rates for each of the $12$ heads, while the decay head predicts $12$ head-wise retention factors $\alpha$ . During readout, the retrieved features are processed by an RMSNorm layer followed by a linear projection back to the output feature space. This design represents the pose-related temporal state directly in the model parameters rather than maintaining a large set of pose-memory tokens.

#### Channel-wise state update module.

The channel-wise state update module regulates how new observations are incorporated into the explicit geometric state and contains approximately $0.98$ M parameters. Specifically, it concatenates the $768$ -dimensional historical state feature with the $1024$ -dimensional current visual feature, resulting in a $1792$ -dimensional input. The concatenated feature is projected to a bottleneck dimension of $384$ , followed by a GELU activation and a second linear projection to $768$ dimensions. A sigmoid function is then applied element-wise to produce the channel-wise update gate, allowing different feature channels to adaptively retain historical information or absorb new observations.

#### Source of the parameter reduction.

The parameter reduction primarily comes from replacing the entire pose-related LocalMemory module of CUT3R. In the CUT3R configuration used in our experiments, the encoder and decoder feature dimensions are $\texttt{enc\_embed\_dim}=1024$ and $\texttt{dec\_embed\_dim}=768$ , respectively, with $\texttt{local\_mem\_size}=256$ . The LocalMemory first projects the $1024$ -dimensional encoder feature to $768$ dimensions and concatenates it with a $768$ -dimensional pose feature. Consequently, each LocalMemory decoder block operates at a feature dimension of

$$ d_{L}=2\times 768=1536. $$

CUT3R employs two Transformer blocks for memory writing and another two blocks for memory readout, resulting in four LocalMemory decoder blocks in total.

For each decoder block, the self-attention projections contain approximately $4d_{L}^{2}\approx 9.44$ M parameters, and the cross-attention projections contribute another $4d_{L}^{2}\approx 9.44$ M parameters. The feed-forward network uses a hidden dimension of $4d_{L}$ and therefore contains approximately $8d_{L}^{2}\approx 18.87$ M parameters. The dominant parameter count of each block is thus

$$ 4d_{L}^{2}+4d_{L}^{2}+8d_{L}^{2}=16d_{L}^{2}\approx 37.75\text{M}, $$

or approximately $37.78$ M when biases and normalization parameters are included. The four memory-writing and memory-readout blocks therefore account for approximately $151.12$ M parameters. Together with the additional query projection, the learnable local memory of size $256\times 1536$ , and the masked token, the complete pose-related LocalMemory module contains approximately $152.31$ M parameters.

#### Overall complexity.

Our design removes this $152.31$ M-parameter pose-related LocalMemory module and replaces it with the fast-weight pose memory and the channel-wise state update module, which contain approximately $1.56$ M and $0.98$ M parameters, respectively. The two proposed modules therefore introduce only approximately

$$ 1.56\text{M}+0.98\text{M}=2.54\text{M} $$

parameters in total. This yields a net parameter reduction of approximately

$$ 152.31\text{M}-2.54\text{M}=149.77\text{M}, $$

which is consistent with the reduction of the full model from approximately $793$ M to $644$ M parameters. These results also support our design motivation: using multiple Transformer decoder blocks together with token-based storage is unnecessarily parameter-intensive for representing a compact $6$ -DoF camera pose state. By replacing this pose-specific token memory with fast weights, our model substantially reduces parameter and memory overhead while achieving stronger long-horizon streaming 3D reconstruction and camera pose estimation performance.

#### Hybrid Memory Update Interval

Given that Mem3R is trained on sequences of up to 64 views, we investigate how the model adapts to significantly longer sequences during inference by varying the memory update interval $n\in\{1,2,4,6,8,10\}$ . We update the implicit and explicit memories only every $n$ -th frame, whereas the ATE is computed across all frames. Frames between two memory updates still produce pose predictions, but they are not used to update either memory. While our primary results in the main paper use a default stride of $n=1$ , we find that an interval of $n=2$ achieves peak performance on the long sequences of TUM Dynamics and ScanNet, as shown in Tab. 5. Larger intervals eventually lead to a decline in accuracy due to the loss of fine-grained temporal information. This trend suggests that less frequent memory updates may improve long-sequence stability by reducing sensitivity to high-frequency frame-level noise and redundant observations. Updating the memory at every frame exposes the model to such noise and redundancy, whereas a moderate stride such as $n=2$ smooths the update process while retaining sufficient temporal resolution for accurate tracking.

### 6.6 Social Impacts

#### Positive Social Impact.

Our real-time streaming 3D reconstruction framework can broaden the applicability of online 3D perception in real-world scenarios. By maintaining a fixed-size memory while improving long-sequence temporal consistency, our model is well suited for applications such as robotics, AR/VR, and embodied agents, where systems need to process continuous visual streams efficiently and reliably. Its improved stability over long sequences may further benefit navigation, scene understanding, and interactive 3D mapping in dynamic real-world environments.

#### Potential Negative Impact.

We do not foresee significant misuse risks specific to our method beyond the general considerations associated with 3D reconstruction and perception technologies. As with other 3D perception systems, deployment in real-world environments may raise privacy concerns if visual streams are collected or processed without user consent, especially in private indoor spaces. In addition, although our model improves long-sequence performance, occasional failure cases may still occur under challenging conditions such as severe motion blur, rapid viewpoint changes, textureless regions, or highly dynamic scenes. Practical deployments should therefore follow standard privacy-preserving data collection practices and include downstream validation mechanisms to detect unreliable predictions.
